chief_complaint: frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and heavy periods
hpi_details: A 35-year-old female presents to the clinic with frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and heavy periods. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks her heavy periods and nosebleeds are just draining her body and causing severe iron deficiency anemia.
concerns: She is terrified that her unexplained bruising means she might have leukemia like her aunt did.
expectations: She hopes to have blood work done today and get a prescription for high-dose iron pills to stop the exhaustion.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Von Willebrand Disease evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Von Willebrand Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management for Von Willebrand Disease emphasizes desmopressin (DDAVP) and avoiding aspirin and NSAIDs, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and heavy periods

Key HPI features: A 35-year-old female presents to the clinic with frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and heavy periods. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for von Willebrand Disease.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Von Willebrand Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Immune thrombocytopenic purpura without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Bleeding severe enough to require transfusion.
management_principles: Plan for von Willebrand Disease: Desmopressin (DDAVP), avoid aspirin and NSAIDs
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and heavy periods. HPI: vWF deficiency.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for von Willebrand Disease.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for von Willebrand Disease.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm the subtype and baseline von Willebrand factor/FVIII studies with hematology. Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs when possible. Use desmopressin only when the subtype and response support it; use von Willebrand factor concentrate for nonresponsive or contraindicated cases and plan menstrual-bleeding management individually.

Select appropriate diagnostic workup for von Willebrand Disease

teaching.one_liner: The most common inherited bleeding disorder, from reduced or dysfunctional von Willebrand factor, causing frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and heavy periods.
red_flags: Bleeding severe enough to require transfusion

must_ask.say: How often do you get nosebleeds, and how long do they last?
Do you bruise more easily than others?
Has this been happening since you were young?
Does anyone in your family have similar bleeding problems?

history.answer: I keep getting nosebleeds and notice random bruises all over my arms and legs, and my periods have been much heavier than usual.
The nosebleeds started a couple of months ago, and each episode usually continues for fifteen to twenty minutes before stopping.
The blood drips out from both nostrils down the front, filling several tissues, but it doesn't run down the back of my throat.
I get nosebleeds about two to three times every week, and it seems to be happening more frequently lately.
I pinch the soft lower part of my nose and lean slightly forward, but it takes fifteen to twenty minutes of steady pressure to stop.
I feel a little lightheaded and tired after bleeding, but I haven't passed out, had cold sweats, or swallowed or vomited any blood.
No, I don't pick my nose, blow it hard, or have any injury to my face, and our indoor air isn't particularly dry.
No, I don't have nasal congestion on either side, foul-smelling mucus, facial pain or numbness, or blocked ears.
Yes, I get large bruises easily from minor bumps, my gums bleed when brushing, and small cuts bleed much longer than normal, though I have not seen blood in my urine or stool.
My periods have become much heavier over the last few months, soaking through pads every hour or two with clots and lasting over seven days.
I have always bruised a little more easily than others, and I had prolonged bleeding when I had my wisdom teeth pulled years ago, but it has definitely worsened recently.
No, I don't take aspirin, warfarin, ibuprofen, other pain relievers, or supplements like ginkgo.
No, I have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure and my readings are always normal.
No history of liver disease or hepatitis, and I only drink an occasional glass of wine.
I have been feeling generalized fatigue and sluggishness, but I have not had any fever, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss.
No crusted sores in my nose, no coughing up blood, and my urine has never looked frothy or red.
No, I have never used nasal steroid sprays, and I do not snort or inhale illicit drugs.
No, I don't have any tiny red dots or spider-like red spots on my lips, tongue, or fingertips.

I thought maybe my iron levels are completely drained or I'm just severely anemic from having such heavy periods. My aunt had random bruises like this right before she was diagnosed with leukemia, so I'm terrified that's what's happening to me.
I'm hoping you can run a blood test today and give me some strong iron supplements so I stop feeling so wiped out.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions or ongoing illnesses.
I have never been hospitalized or had surgery, except for wisdom tooth extraction in my twenties that bled for several days.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter painkillers, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or other substances.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I drink alcohol only socially, perhaps one glass of wine once or twice a month.
I work as an office accountant and live in an apartment with my husband.
My mother has always had very heavy periods and frequent nosebleeds as well, though she was never formally diagnosed with a bleeding disorder.
My last menstrual period started about two weeks ago. My cycle is regular at twenty-eight days, but the flow is very heavy.
We use barrier methods like condoms for contraception, and there is no chance that I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Alert and oriented, appearing mildly fatigued but in no acute distress; sitting comfortably.
Blood pressure 115/75 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Mild conjunctival pallor noted bilaterally; sclerae anicteric without telangiectasias.
Traces of dried blood over the anterior nasal septum bilaterally without active bleeding, mucosal ulceration, or mass; posterior pharynx clear without active blood pooling or trickling.
No palpable cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields without wheezes, crackles, or rhonchi.
Soft, non-tender throughout without guarding or rebound tenderness; liver and spleen are not palpable.
Scattered ecchymoses in various healing stages on the forearms and shins; no petechiae, purpura, or telangiectatic lesions on lips or fingers.
